segments.text:
- Line 1 makes `bash` the interpreter.
- The script runs on CRB (the Arm reference server under test). It builds the binary `bwx12`, runs the self-test of the binary, prints checksums, and saves the machine code of every kernel. A kernel is one inner loop of the benchmark.
- The comment names three earlier versions of this script: `build8.sh`, `build10.sh` and `build11.sh`. Each version keeps the checks of the version before and adds to them.
- This script does not apply the rule of line 4 (a build whose listing differs from the accepted one is rejected). The script that line 22 names applies it.
segments.heading: Header comment: what the script does

segments.text:
- The script takes no argument. Lines 16 to 21 list the six files that it writes into its own folder. The rows below explain each file at the line that writes it.
- `EXTRA` (line 14) was a variable for more compiler flags in the build script of the older runner version bwx [Ref19]. This script has no such variable, so the flags of line 37 are the only flags.
- Line 22 names the step after the build. On the development machine, `check_listing12.py` compares `listing.txt` and `offsets.tsv` with the accepted build of bwx11 (the runner version before bwx12) [Ref10].

Each exit status belongs to one check: 3 to `check_marker` (line 32), 5 to the compiler call (line 47), 4 to the self-test (line 54), 6 to the branch-target check (line 99). Status 0 means that every step ran.
Another failed command can also end the script (rule `-e` of line 30, with the exceptions named there). The exit status is then the status of that command.

The script reads three binaries of older runner versions (bwx8, bwx10, bwx11) with the tool `nm`, and does not run them. `nm` lists the symbols of a binary with their addresses. Three environment variables replace the default paths. A missing file does not stop the script (lines 125 to 127, 137 to 139 and 149 to 151).

`set -euo pipefail` sets three rules for the whole script:
- `-e`: the script ends when a command fails. A command that `if` tests, or that `||` follows, does not end it. The form `$( )` runs commands and inserts their output. A failed command inside `$( )` ends the script only when the `$( )` is the whole right side of an assignment (line 64). It does not end the script when the `$( )` stands inside an `echo` text (line 41) or a `for` list (line 62). Bash also turns `-e` off inside `$( )`, and every call of `placement` stands inside `$( )`. So a failed `nm` (line 109) does not end the script.
- `-u`: the script ends when it uses a variable that was never set.
- `-o pipefail`: a pipeline counts as failed when any of its commands fails, not only the last one.
segments.heading: Shell options

segments.text:
- `MARKER` is the path of the marker file, by default `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. Another user creates this file during a performance test [Ref18]. The environment variable `BWX_MARKER` replaces the path (for a test of this check).
- `check_marker` tests whether the file exists (`-e`). If it exists, the function prints a message to the error output (`>&2`) and ends the script with status 3.
- Line 33 is the first call. Line 50 and line 61 call it again, each time before the script runs the new binary.
segments.heading: Function `check_marker`: stop when the marker file exists

segments.text:
- On the first pass the variable `_PINNED` is empty, so the `if` branch runs.
- `exec` replaces the shell with `taskset`, and `taskset` starts this script again (`$0`) with the same arguments (`$@`).
- `taskset -c 0-119` limits a program to CPUs 0 to 119. bwx12.c names this range as the rule of the test machine [Ref8].
- `_PINNED=1` goes into the environment of the new run. So the second pass skips the `if` branch and continues with line 35.
- Every program that the script starts later inherits the limit: the compiler, the new binary, `objdump` and `nm`.
- The environment variable `BWX_CPUS` replaces the list `0-119`.
segments.heading: CPU limit: the script restarts itself under `taskset`

segments.text: `SRC` is the absolute path of the folder that holds this script: `cd` goes to the folder of `$0`, and `pwd` prints it. `CC` is the compiler: the environment variable `CC` if it is set and not empty, otherwise `gcc`. The CRB build used gcc 14.2.0 [Ref1].

The same gcc 14.2.0 built bw_old and bw_new (the two binaries of the benchmark of 2026-11-13) with the first seven flags. The last three flags were not used for bw_old and bw_new [Ref15] [Ref16].
- `-O3`: the highest numbered optimization level of gcc. The compiler may inline functions and vectorize loops [Ref17]. In the CRB build the 16 sums of the old read kernel are 8 vector adds per loop pass of `k_oldread` [Ref3].
- `-march=native`: gcc picks the architecture of the machine on which the build runs. The architecture decides which instructions the compiler may use [Ref22]. The build ran on CRB. Example: the machine code of `timed_sequence` holds SVE instructions (SVE is a vector extension of Arm) [Ref4]. The flag names no processor to tune for, and line 37 holds no `-mtune` and no `-mcpu`. For that case the gcc manual says that the code is tuned to perform well on a range of processors of that architecture [Ref22].
- `-fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns`: gcc does not turn a loop pattern into a call of a library function [Ref17]. A store loop that becomes a call of `memset` is such a pattern. In the CRB build `k_oldwrite` and `k_oldcopy` are loops, and no kernel calls a library function for its work [Ref3].
- `-pthread`: compile and link with support for POSIX threads. bwx12 runs its benchmark threads as POSIX threads [Ref8].
- `-Wall -Wextra`: turn on most warnings of the compiler, and some more [Ref17]. A warning does not stop the build. It is written into `build.txt` (line 47). The CRB build has none [Ref1].
- `-std=gnu11`: the source is compiled as C of the 2011 standard with the GNU extensions [Ref17].
- `-fno-ipa-icf`: gcc does not merge two functions that have identical code [Ref17]. bwx12.c holds kernels that are one source under two names, for example `oldread` and `oldread2`. With this flag gcc keeps both [Ref8].
- `-fno-toplevel-reorder`: gcc writes the functions and the top-level `asm` statements into the binary in the order of the source file [Ref17]. bwx12.c needs this for its macro `PLACE`, which puts padding bytes directly before a kernel [Ref8].
- `-falign-functions=4`: gcc aligns the start of a function to 4 bytes only. Then a kernel starts directly after the pad of `PLACE`, at the planned address modulo 64 [Ref8].
segments.heading: Compiler flags, one by one

segments.text:
`b` is the name of the binary. `B` is the path of `build.txt`. The block writes four lines and replaces an older `build.txt` (`>`):
- `## host=... utc=... load_before=... logins=...`: the host name, the UTC time at the start, the load averages of the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (fields 1 to 3 of `/proc/loadavg`), and the number of lines that `who` prints (one line per login session).
- `## cc=...`: the first line of the version text of the compiler.
- `## CFLAGS=...`: the flags of line 37.
- `## compiler messages:`: a title for the text that the compiler prints next.
- CRB build: host `ubuntu`, start at 17:12:11 UTC on 2026-11-15, load averages 1.18, 28.51 and 31.03 tasks (1, 5 and 15 minutes), 0 logins [Ref1].
segments.heading: Record `build.txt`: the first four lines

segments.text:
- The compiler builds `bwx12.c` into the binary `bwx12` in the folder of the script. `bwx12.c` includes `bwx12_selftest.c` with `#include`, so one compiler call is enough [Ref8].
- `$CFLAGS` has no quotes on purpose: the shell must split it into single flags. Line 46 tells the checking tool shellcheck not to warn about that.
- `>> "$B" 2>&1` appends every message of the compiler to `build.txt`.
- If the compiler fails, the part after `||` prints `build.txt` to the error output and ends the script with status 5.
- Line 48 appends the line `## compiler messages end`.
- CRB build: nothing stands between the two `compiler messages` lines, so the compiler printed no warning [Ref1].
segments.heading: Compile `bwx12.c`

segments.text:
- Line 50 checks the marker file again. Line 51 is the first run of the new binary.
- `bwx12 --selftest` runs the self-test. Its whole output goes to `selftest-bwx12.txt` (`2>&1` adds the error output).
- The self-test calls each of the 55 kernels on buffers of 1 page, 3 pages and 1 MiB, and on single blocks of 256 B. Before each of these calls it prints a line that begins with `call,`. After each call it checks the memory. Then it tests the trial mode. Each check prints one row that ends with `pass` or `FAIL` [Ref9].
- Limit: for a read kernel that returns nothing, the self-test shows that the buffer is unchanged and that the kernel touches every page of a 3-page range. It does not show that the kernel reads every byte [Ref9]. In the CRB build the rows of `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl` hold these two kinds of check only. The rows of `oldread` also hold the check that the returned sum equals the sum of all words [Ref5].
- Exit status 0: the script appends `## selftest bwx12 exit=0` plus the last line of the self-test output to `build.txt`. CRB build: `# failures=0`, and 457 rows end with `pass` [Ref1] [Ref5].
- Any other status: the script appends `## selftest bwx12 exit=N` (N is the status), prints the last 3 lines of the output to the error output, and ends with status 4.
segments.heading: Self-test of the new binary

segments.text: Line 59 empties `listing.txt`: the command `:` does nothing, and `>` creates the file or makes it empty (0 bytes). Line 60 writes the header line of `offsets.tsv`: six column names with tabs between them. Line 62 runs the binary once more. So line 61 checks the marker file again before it.
segments.heading: Records `listing.txt` and `offsets.tsv`: machine code of every kernel

segments.text:
- `bwx12 --list` prints the names of all kernels, one per line (55 in the CRB build [Ref2]). The loop runs once per name `k`. `fn` is the function of the kernel: `k_` plus the name.
- A failed `--list` run does not end the script (see the row of line 30). The loop then runs over the names that the binary printed before it failed. In the CRB build the loop got every name. The first line of the self-test output gives `kernels=55`. `offsets.tsv` has 55 kernel rows [Ref2] [Ref5].
- `objdump -d --disassemble=$fn` prints the machine code of this one function as assembler text. It stops at the end of the function. `--no-show-raw-insn` leaves out the bytes of each instruction.
- `sed -n '/>:$/,/^$/p'` keeps the lines from the label line of the function (it ends with `>:`) to the next empty line. This drops the header that `objdump` prints first.
- Line 65 appends three things to `listing.txt`: the title line `=== bwx12 <kernel> ===`, the text of the function, and an empty line.
- The listing holds the six kernels of the whole-chip test: `oldread`, `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl` [Ref3].

These lines find the start of the function and the start of its loop.
- Line 66: `start` is the address on the label line (line 1 of the text), without leading zeros. `loop` and `mod` begin as `NA`.
- Line 73 gives the instruction lines to the `while` loop as input: every line after the first that begins with a hexadecimal address and a colon. `read` puts the address into `addr` and the rest of the line into `rest`. Line 68 removes the colon.
- Line 69 looks for a branch to a place inside the same function. `objdump` prints such a target as an address and a name, for example `49a4 <k_read+0x4>`. `tgt` is that address.
- Line 71 compares the addresses as hexadecimal numbers (`16#`). The branch goes backward when the target is lower than the address of the branch instruction and not lower than `start`. Then `loop` is the target, `mod` is the target modulo 64 as a decimal number, and `break` ends the search.
- So the loop start is the target of the first backward branch. If a function had two loops, only the first would be recorded. In the CRB build each of the 55 kernel functions holds exactly one backward branch to an address inside the function [Ref3].

Line 74 appends one row per kernel to `offsets.tsv`, with tabs between the six fields:
- `binary`: always `bwx12`. `kernel`: the kernel name. `function`: `k_` plus that name.
- `start`: the address of the first instruction of the function, hexadecimal.
- `loop_start`: the address of the first instruction of the loop, hexadecimal. It is `NA` when the function has no backward branch.
- `loop_mod64`: `loop_start` modulo 64, a decimal number of bytes from 0 to 63. It is the offset of the loop start inside a 64-byte block of code.
- CRB build: `oldread` has `start` 4600, `loop_start` 4668 (both hexadecimal) and `loop_mod64` 40 bytes. `read` has 49a0, 49a4 and 36 bytes. `asmread` has 4ac0, 4ad4 and 20 bytes. No row holds `NA` [Ref2].

- The comment gives the rule. `timed_sequence` and `timed_sequence_hot` may branch only to four places: `clock_gettime` (the clock read), a kernel (through a function pointer), `tcount` (a function of bwx12.c that reads the event counters), and the stack-guard failure function.
- Both functions belong to the trial mode of bwx12 (option `--trial`). They time the windows of a trial [Ref8].
- The whole-chip test does not use the trial mode. Its spec files start bwx12 with `--seq`. Then the function `worker` of bwx12.c times each interval [Ref8] [Ref13].
- So this check does not cover the timed path of the whole-chip test. This script does not save the machine code of `worker`.
- Line 83 empties `seq-listing.txt`. `seq_fail=0` means that no function has failed yet.
segments.heading: Check with exit status 6: branch targets of the trial-mode timed functions

segments.text: The loop runs once for each of the two functions. Line 86 stores the whole `objdump` output for the function in `code`. Line 87 appends to `seq-listing.txt` the title line `=== bwx12 <function> ===`, the text of the function (label line to the next empty line) and an empty line. Apart from the checksum of line 155, no script reads `seq-listing.txt` (line 21): it is for a person to read.

The pipeline lists the places outside the function that the function calls or branches to, each with a count.
- First `awk` rule (line 89): skip every line that does not begin with an address and a colon.
- Second rule (line 90): an indirect call or jump prints `(indirect)`. On Arm these are the instructions `blr` and `br` (branch to the address in a register). The `call` and `jmp` patterns are x86 mnemonics.
- Third rule (lines 91 and 92): it handles a call or branch instruction whose last field is a name in angle brackets. It prints the name without the brackets, without an offset such as `+0x2c0`, and without `@plt`. It does not print the name of the function itself, so a branch inside the function does not count.
- `LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c` sorts the names and counts each name. `LC_ALL=C` makes `sort` compare plain byte values.
- The last `awk` joins the names into one line of `name=count` pairs with one space between them.
- `objdump` adds a comment such as `// b.any` after some conditional branches. Then the last field is not a name, and the third rule skips the line. In the saved listing every such branch stays inside its own function [Ref4].

- Line 93 appends the list to `build.txt` as `## <function> branch targets: ...`. An empty list is written as `none`.
- CRB build, the same for both functions: `(indirect)=4 __stack_chk_fail=1 clock_gettime=2 tcount=2`. Each number counts the instructions that go to that target [Ref1].
- Line 94 collects the names that are not allowed in `seq_bad`. `tr` puts each `name=count` pair on its own line, and `sed` removes `=count`. `grep -vxE` keeps the lines that are not exactly one of the four allowed names.
- `|| true` stops the rule `-e` from ending the script when `grep` keeps no line (`grep` then returns status 1).

- A function fails in three cases: `seq_bad` holds a name, the list has no `clock_gettime=` entry, or the list has no `(indirect)=` entry. In the last two cases the function would not read the clock or would not call a kernel.
- On failure, line 96 prints the list to the error output and sets `seq_fail=1`. The loop still handles the second function, so `seq-listing.txt` and `build.txt` hold both.
- Line 99 then ends the script with status 6 if a function failed. In that case `build.txt` gets no placement lines and no sha256 lines.

`placement FILE` prints one line of `name=value` pairs for a binary.
- `nm` lists the symbols of the binary with their addresses. `2>/dev/null` hides its error messages.
- `awk` keeps the symbols with the names `call`, `read_smaps`, `tcount`, `timed_sequence` and `timed_sequence_hot`, and prints name and address.
- `LC_ALL=C sort` sorts the lines by name. `LC_ALL=C` makes `sort` compare plain byte values.
- The `while` loop prints each name with its address modulo 64, in decimal. This is the offset of the function start inside a 64-byte block, in bytes.
- Line 111 prints the result without the space at its end.
- Purpose (comment): bwx12.c adds padding after its new kernels. The goal is that these functions start at the same offset as in the older binaries [Ref8]. The result is a record: a difference does not stop the build.
segments.heading: Function `placement`: where five functions start, modulo 64

segments.text:
- `BWX8_BIN` is the path of the accepted binary of bwx8. The default is the file `bwx8` in the folder `bwx8-20261114`, which stands beside the folder of this script.
- `p12` is the placement line of the new binary. Line 115 appends it to `build.txt` (`none` if it is empty).
- CRB build: `call=24 read_smaps=52 tcount=52 timed_sequence=28 timed_sequence_hot=32` [Ref1]. For example, `call` starts 24 bytes after a 64-byte boundary.
- A name in this line shows that the binary holds a symbol for the function. It does not show that any code calls it. In a test of this task, gcc 11.4.0 with `-O3 -fno-toplevel-reorder` kept the symbol of a `static` function that it had inlined at its only call [Ref21]. So with that compiler the rule of the comment of lines 102 and 103 does not hold for every function. The CRB compiler (gcc 14.2.0) was not tested.
segments.heading: Placement record and comparison with three older binaries

segments.text:
- If the bwx8 binary exists (`-f`), the script appends its placement line and then one line with the result of the comparison.
- bwx8 has no `timed_sequence_hot`, and this name is the last one in the sorted line. So line 120 removes the last pair from the bwx12 line with `sed` and compares the rest with the bwx8 line as text.
- The result line ends with `same` or `DIFFERS`. An empty bwx8 line gives `DIFFERS`.
- If the file is missing, line 126 appends `not compared` with the path.
- CRB build: `same` [Ref1].

The same steps for the accepted binary of bwx10 (default: the file `bwx10` in the folder `bwx10-20261115`). The bwx10 line of the CRB build has all five functions, and line 132 compares the two whole lines. CRB build: `same` [Ref1].

The same steps for the accepted binary of bwx11 (default: the file `bwx11` in the folder `bwx11-20261115`). CRB build: `same` [Ref1]. So in the CRB build the five functions of bwx12 start at the same offsets as in bwx10 and bwx11, and the first four at the same offsets as in bwx8.

The block appends the end of `build.txt`:
- `## sha256:`, then one line per file from `sha256sum`: the sha256 value (a checksum of 64 hexadecimal digits) and the file name. `cd` goes to the folder of the script first, so the names carry no path. The parentheses limit this `cd` to the one command line.
- The seven files are `bwx12.c`, `bwx12_selftest.c`, this script, the binary, `listing.txt`, `offsets.tsv` and `seq-listing.txt`. `build.txt` and `selftest-bwx12.txt` get no line.
- `## load_after=... utc=...`: the three load averages and the UTC time at the end.
- CRB build: the value of the binary begins with `cd58e564`. `go.sh` of the whole-chip test holds the full value and passes it to `rx.sh`. Both scripts check it and do not start a `bwx12` file with another value [Ref11] [Ref12].
- CRB build: end at 17:12:14 UTC, 3 s after the start, with load averages 1.17, 28.05 and 30.86 tasks [Ref1].
segments.heading: Last records: sha256 values, load and end time

segments.text: The script prints `build.txt`, then the line `## offsets.tsv:`, then `offsets.tsv` to the standard output. For the CRB build the file `build.out` in the folder `crb-build-1` holds this text: the 24 lines of `build.txt`, the title line, and the 56 lines of `offsets.tsv` [Ref6].
